title: What helps the dead
translation: Jōganbō, the priest from Takedani, once went to see the empress Higashi Nijō-in. She asked him: "When we hold services for the dead, what does them the most good?" He answered: "The Mantra of Light, and the Treasure Casket spell."
Afterwards his disciples asked him: "Why did you say that? Why didn't you tell her that nothing beats chanting Amida's name?"

"It's our own school," he said, "so of course I wanted to. But I've never seen a sutra that says clearly that chanting the name for the dead does them great good. If she had asked me, 'Where does it say that?', what would I have told her? So I went with what the scriptures clearly back up, and named the mantra and the spell."
original: {竹谷|たけだに}の{乗願房|じようぐわんばう}、{東二条院|とうにでうのゐん}へ{参|まゐ}られたりけるに、「{亡者|まうじや}の{追善|ついぜん}には{何事|なにごと}か{勝利|しようり}{多|おほ}き。」と{尋|たづ}ねさせ{給|たま}ひければ、「{光明真言|くわうみやうしんごん}、{宝篋印陀羅尼|ほうけふいんだらに}。」と{申|まう}されたりけるを、
{弟子|でし}ども、「いかにかくは{申|まう}し{給|たま}ひけるぞ。
{念仏|ねんぶつ}に{勝|まさ}ること{候|さうらふ}まじとは、など{申|まう}し{給|たま}はぬぞ。」と{申|まう}しければ、
「わが{宗|しゆう}なれば、さこそ{申|まう}さまほしかりつれども、まさしく{称名|しやうみやう}を{追福|ついふく}に{修|しゆ}して{巨益|こやく}あるべしと{説|と}ける{経文|きやうもん}を{見|み}{及|およ}ばねば、
{何|なに}に{見|み}えたるぞと、{重|かさ}ねて{問|と}はせ{給|たま}はば、いかが{申|まう}さむとおもひて、{本経|ほんぎやう}のたしかなるにつきて、この{真言|しんごん}、{陀羅尼|だらに}をば{申|まう}しつるなり。」とぞ{申|まう}されける。
literal: When Jōganbō of Takedani visited the Higashi Nijō-in, she asked, 'For memorial services for the dead, what has the greatest merit?', and he answered, 'The Mantra of Light, the Hōkyōin dhāraṇī'; at this,
his disciples said, 'Why did you answer like that?
Why did you not say that there is nothing better than the nenbutsu?', and he said,
'Since it is my own school, I did want to say so, but since I have never come across a sutra passage that clearly teaches that calling the Name, practised for the dead, brings great benefit,
I thought, if she asked again "Where is that written?", what could I say? So I went by what has a sure basis in scripture and named this mantra and dhāraṇī,' he said.

notes.text: The 1925 edition explains Takedani as a place at Daigo, south-east of Kyoto, and Jōganbō as a Pure Land priest who lived there. {房|ばう} at the end of a name marks a priest. Commentators usually take him to be a disciple of Hōnen, the founder of the Pure Land school.
Saionji Kimiko (1232–1304), the empress of Emperor Go-Fukakusa, as the edition notes. {尋|たづ}ねさせ{給|たま}ひ and {問|と}はせ{給|たま}は use double honorifics, the level of respect for an empress.
A false friend: {勝利|しようり} here is Buddhist 'merit, benefit', what a rite does for the soul. Modern {勝利|しようり} is 'victory'. {追善|ついぜん} and {追福|ついふく}: rites done by the living to send merit to the dead.

notes.quote: 光明真言、宝篋印陀羅尼
notes.text: Two spells of the Shingon (esoteric) school, as the edition notes: formulas in Sanskrit sounds, recited for the dead. The Mantra of Light ({光明真言|くわうみやうしんごん}) and the Hōkyōin ('Treasure Casket Seal') dhāraṇī. Neither is a Pure Land practice.

notes.quote: 念仏に勝ること候まじ
notes.text: {念仏|ねんぶつ}: chanting 'Namu Amida Butsu', calling on the Buddha Amida. For the Pure Land school it is the one practice that matters. {称名|しやうみやう}, 'calling the name', in his answer is the same thing. まじ: 'surely not'. The disciples speak politely, with {候|さうらふ}.

notes.quote: さこそ申さまほしかりつれども
notes.text: まほし: 'want to'. こそ … ども: 'I did want to, but…'. He admits the wish and then explains why he did not follow it.

notes.quote: 本経のたしかなるにつきて
notes.text: {本経|ほんぎやう}: the sutra that is the source of a practice. He answers only with what he can back up from a text.
The section ends with his answer. Kenkō adds no comment.
